claim: 3-hydroxypropylglucosinolate (3OHPGSL) causes root meristem inhibition in Arabidopsis at concentrations down to 1 µM.
source: We found that 3OHPGSL causes root meristem inhibition, at concentrations down to 1 µM (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing dose-dependent root growth inhibition in Figure 1A-B.

claim: The 3OHPGSL response is concentration-dependent.
source: The observed response is concentration-dependent (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental measurements across different concentrations shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: All Arabidopsis accessions accumulate 3OHPGSL in the seeds, and this pool is maintained at early seedling stages.
source: All Arabidopsis accessions accumulate 3OHPGSL in the seeds, and this pool is maintained at early seedling stages (Chan et al., 2011; Petersen et al., 2002; Brown et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: GSLs in the seed are primarily deposited in the embryo, accumulating to about 3µmol/g.
source: Previous research has shown that GSLs in the seed are primarily deposited in the embryo, accumulating to about 3µmol/g suggesting that we are working with concentrations within the endogenous physiological range (Fang et al., 2012; Kliebenstein et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Col-0 without treatment had average foliar levels of 3OHPGSL of 3.2 µmol/g.
source: Col-0 without treatment had average foliar levels of 3OHPGSL of 3.2 µmol/g and grown on media containing 5 µM, 3OHPGSL contributed an additional 2.2 µmol/g raising the total 3OHPGSL to 5.4 µmol/g (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Exogenous 3OHPGSL application (5 µM) contributed an additional 2.2 µmol/g to Col-0 foliar tissue, raising total 3OHPGSL to 5.4 µmol/g.
source: Col-0 without treatment had average foliar levels of 3OHPGSL of 3.2 µmol/g and grown on media containing 5 µM, 3OHPGSL contributed an additional 2.2 µmol/g raising the total 3OHPGSL to 5.4 µmol/g (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The myb28-1 myb29-1 mutant had no measurable 3OHPGSL on control plates and accumulated ~1.4µmol/g upon treatment.
source: The myb28-1 myb29-1 mutant had no measurable 3OHPGSL on the control plates and accumulated ~1.4µmol/g upon treatment (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The myb28-1 myb29-1 mutant had a lower root growth response to exogenous 3OHPGSL compared to wild-type.
source: In agreement with the lower foliar 3OHPGSL accumulation in the myb28-1 myb29-1 mutant background, this double mutant had a lower root growth response to exogenous 3OHPGSL (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Even during prolonged exposures up to 14 days, Col-0 seedlings continued being vital and green when exposed to 3OHPGSL.
source: The first evidence against toxicity came from the observation that even during prolonged exposures, up to 14 days of length, Col-0 seedlings continued being vital and green (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Root inhibition by 50 µM 3OHPGSL is reversible.
source: Importantly, root inhibition is reversible, as the 3OHPGSL-mediated root stunting could be switched on and off by transfer between control media and media containing 3OHPGSL (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental transfer experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 3-methylsulfinyl-propyl (3MSP) GSL does not possess root-inhibiting activities within the tested concentration range.
source: In contrast to 3OHPGSL, neither of these structurally related GSLs possessed similar root-inhibiting activities within the tested concentration range (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Allyl GSL does not possess root-inhibiting activities within the tested concentration range.
source: In contrast to 3OHPGSL, neither of these structurally related GSLs possessed similar root-inhibiting activities within the tested concentration range (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: 4-methylsulfinylbutyl (4MSB) GSL cannot inhibit root growth at the tested concentrations.
source: Neither of these compounds could inhibit root growth at the tested concentrations (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F-H.

claim: But-3-enyl GSL cannot inhibit root growth at the tested concentrations.
source: Neither of these compounds could inhibit root growth at the tested concentrations (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F-H.

claim: Neither the R nor S form of 2-hydroxybut-3-enylGSL was similar to 3OHPGSL and both actually stimulated root growth.
source: This showed that neither enantiomer was similar to 3OHPGSL and that both actually stimulated root growth (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only 3OHPGSL inhibits root elongation among the tested GSLs, suggesting that the core GSL structure does not cause the effect.
source: The fact that only 3OHPGSL inhibits root elongation suggests that the core GSL structure (comprised of a sulfate and thioglucose) does not cause the effect.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of structurally related GSLs.

claim: 3OHPGSL root inhibition is not a generic result of providing extra sulfur or glucose from the GSL core structure to the plant.
source: Importantly, this indicates that 3OHPGSL root inhibition is not a generic result of providing extra sulfur or glucose from the GSL core structure to the plant, as these compounds would be equally contributed by the other GSLs.
evidence: Inferred from the specificity of 3OHPGSL effect compared to other GSLs.

claim: There is no general toxic activity when applying GSLs to Arabidopsis.
source: Furthermore, the results confirm that there is no general toxic activity when applying GSLs to Arabidopsis.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of different GSLs.

claim: The 3OHPGSL root inhibition effect links to the specific 3OHP side chain structure.
source: This evidence argues that the 3OHPGSL root inhibition effect links to the specific 3OHP side chain structure, indicating the presence of a specific molecular target mediating the root inhibition response.
evidence: Inferred from the structural specificity of the response.

claim: The evolution of the GSL defense system occurred within the last ~92 Ma and is largely limited to the Brassicales order.
source: The evolution of the GSL defense system is a relatively young phylogenetic event that occurred within the last ~92 Ma and is largely limited to the Brassicales order (Edger et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The aliphatic GSL pathway is ~60 Ma old and is limited to the Brassicaceae family.
source: The aliphatic GSL pathway is younger still (~60 Ma) and is limited to the Brassicaceae family with the enzyme required for 3OHPGSL production, AOP3, being limited to Arabidopsis thaliana and Arabidopsis lyrata within the Arabidopsis lineage (Edger et al., 2015; Kliebenstein et al., 2001a).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The enzyme required for 3OHPGSL production, AOP3, is limited to Arabidopsis thaliana and Arabidopsis lyrata within the Arabidopsis lineage.
source: The aliphatic GSL pathway is younger still (~60 Ma) and is limited to the Brassicaceae family with the enzyme required for 3OHPGSL production, AOP3, being limited to Arabidopsis thaliana and Arabidopsis lyrata within the Arabidopsis lineage (Edger et al., 2015; Kliebenstein et al., 2001a).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: 3OHPGSL is found in the vegetative tissue of Olimarabidopsis pumila (dwarf rocket).
source: However, 3OHPGSL is also found in the vegetative tissue of the close relative Olimarabidopsis pumila (dwarf rocket) (Windsor et al., 2005), and in seeds of more distant Brassicaceae family members such as the hawkweed-leaved treacle mustard (Erysimum hieracifolium), virginia stock (Malcolmia maritima), shepherd's cress (Teesdalia nudicaulis), and alpine pennycress (Thlaspi alpestre) (Daxenbichler et al., 1980; Daxenbichler et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: 3OHPGSL is found in seeds of Erysimum hieracifolium, Malcolmia maritima, Teesdalia nudicaulis, and Thlaspi alpestre.
source: However, 3OHPGSL is also found in the vegetative tissue of the close relative Olimarabidopsis pumila (dwarf rocket) (Windsor et al., 2005), and in seeds of more distant Brassicaceae family members such as the hawkweed-leaved treacle mustard (Erysimum hieracifolium), virginia stock (Malcolmia maritima), shepherd's cress (Teesdalia nudicaulis), and alpine pennycress (Thlaspi alpestre) (Daxenbichler et al., 1980; Daxenbichler et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Four of the five tested Brassicales species responded to 5 µM 3OHPGSL with root growth inhibition regardless of their ability to synthesize 3OHPGSL.
source: We found that four of the five tested Brassicales species responded to 5 µM 3OHPGSL with root growth inhibition regardless of their ability to synthesize 3OHPGSL (Figure 3B–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-F.

claim: 5 µM 3OHPGSL can inhibit root growth in several non-Brassicales eudicot species tested.
source: We expanded the survey by including plants within the eudicot lineage that do not have the biosynthetic capacity to produce any GSLs (Figure 3G) and found that 5 µM 3OHPGSL can inhibit root growth in several of the non-Brassicales species tested (Figure 3H–L).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H-L.

claim: 3OHPGSL led to slower log phase growth in Saccharomyces cerevisiae compared to untreated control.
source: The ability of 3OHPGSL to alter growth extended to Saccharomyces cerevisae where 3OHPGSL led to slower log phase growth than the untreated control (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Allyl GSL in the media had no effect on S. cerevisiae growth.
source: Allyl GSL in the media had no effect on S. cerevisae growth showing that this was a 3OHPGSL mediated process (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 3OHPGSL responsiveness is evolutionarily older than the ability to synthesize 3OHPGSL.
source: The observation that 3OHPGSL responsiveness is evolutionarily older than the ability to synthesize 3OHPGSL suggests that the molecular target of
evidence: Inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of 3OHPGSL responsiveness versus biosynthetic capacity.

claim: Root meristems of 3OHPGSL treated seedlings were significantly reduced in cell number compared to untreated controls.
source: Root meristems of 3OHPGSL treated seedlings were significantly reduced in cell number compared to untreated controls (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: 3OHPGSL treatment caused premature initiation of the differentiation zone, as the first root hairs were closer to the root tip.
source: Moreover, we also observed a premature initiation of the differentiation zone, as the first root hairs were closer to the root tip upon 3OHPGSL treatment (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Bulging and branching of root hairs was observed in 3OHPGSL treated roots.
source: In addition, we saw bulging and branching of the root hairs in 3OHPGSL treated roots (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4F.

claim: There was no morphological evidence of cell death in any root treated with 3OHPGSL.
source: There was no morphological evidence of cell death in any root supporting the argument that 3OHPGSL is not a toxin.
evidence: Based on morphological observations from confocal microscopy.

claim: 3OHPGSL leads to root growth inhibition by reducing the size of the meristematic zone within the developing Arabidopsis root.
source: These results indicate that 3OHPGSL leads to root growth inhibition by reducing the size of the meristematic zone within the developing Arabidopsis root.
evidence: Inferred from the cellular morphology data.

claim: The GK548 TORox line exhibits accelerated TORC signaling and grows longer roots on media containing sucrose.
source: The GK548 TORox line exhibits accelerated TORC signaling and consequently grows longer roots on media containing sucrose (Figure 5 and (Deprost et al., 2007)).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5 and citation to previous research.

claim: GK548 TORox meristems are harder to arrest.
source: In addition, GK548 TORox meristems are harder to arrest (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The GK548 TORox line had an elevated 3OHPGSL-mediated inhibition of meristem reactivation in comparison to the WT.
source: Applying 3OHPGSL to the GK548 TORox line showed that this genotype had an elevated 3OHPGSL-mediated inhibition of meristem reactivation in comparison to the WT (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: RAPTOR1 and TOR null mutants are lethal as homozygotes.
source: RAPTOR1 and TOR null mutants are lethal as homozygotes (Menand et al., 2002; Deprost et al., 2005), and heterozygous raptor1 mutants did not display a significant change in 3OHPGSL responsiveness (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research and experimental data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Heterozygous raptor1 mutants did not display a significant change in 3OHPGSL responsiveness.
source: RAPTOR1 and TOR null mutants are lethal as homozygotes (Menand et al., 2002; Deprost et al., 2005), and heterozygous raptor1 mutants did not display a significant change in 3OHPGSL responsiveness (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The raptor2 null mutant is viable and shows mildly reduced root length on sucrose-containing media.
source: We therefore tested insertion mutants within the weaker homolog RAPTOR2, whose null mutant is viable, and in our conditions shows mildly reduced root length on sucrose-containing media (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and C.

claim: For two independent insertion lines raptor2-1 and raptor2-2, there was a statistically significant reduction in 3OHPGSL response.
source: We found that, for two independent insertion lines raptor2-1 (Deprost et al., 2005; Anderson et al., 2005) and raptor2-2 (Deprost et al., 2005) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3E), there was a statistically significant reduction in 3OHPGSL response (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A-C and citations to previous research.

claim: 3OHPGSL could inhibit meristem reactivation of sugar-depleted and photosynthesis-constrained seedlings.
source: By treating arrested root meristems with sucrose alone or in combination with 3OHPGSL we found that 3OHPGSL could inhibit meristem reactivation of sugar-depleted and photosynthesis-constrained seedlings (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: The 3OHPGSL inhibition of meristem reactivation was dependent upon the 3OHPGSL concentration utilized.
source: Further, this response was dependent upon the 3OHPGSL concentration utilized.
evidence: Inferred from the dose-response experiments.

claim: The active site TOR inhibitor AZD-8055 (AZD) induces a reversible concentration-dependent root meristem inhibition.
source: Similar to 3OHPGSL, the active-site TOR inhibitor AZD-8055 (AZD) induces a reversible concentration-dependent root meristem inhibition (Montané and Menand, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: There is a significant antagonistic interaction between AZD and 3OHPGSL in terms of root length response.
source: This identified a significant antagonistic interaction between AZD and 3OHPGSL (3OHP x AZD), both in terms of root length response (Figure 7A) and in initiation of the differentiation zone (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: There is a significant antagonistic interaction between AZD and 3OHPGSL in terms of initiation of the differentiation zone.
source: This identified a significant antagonistic interaction between AZD and 3OHPGSL (3OHP x AZD), both in terms of root length response (Figure 7A) and in initiation of the differentiation zone (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: The premature initiation of the differentiation zone in the presence of 10 µM 3OHPGSL did not change further upon co-treatment with AZD.
source: This antagonistic interaction is also supported by the appearance of first root hair (Figure 7B), as the premature initiation of the differentiation zone in the presence of 10 µM 3OHPGSL did not change further upon co-treatment (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: There is a vast overlap in the phenotypic response to both AZD and 3OHPGSL compounds.
source: Moreover, there was a vast overlap in the phenotypic response to both compounds (Figure 7C–D); notably the closer initiation of the root differentiation zone to the root tip (Figure 7B–C) and the decreased cell elongation (Figure 7C, right panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: 3OHPGSL treatment is phenotypically similar to a range of TOR active site inhibitors and an inhibitor of S6K1.
source: Supporting this is the observation that 3OHPGSL treatment is phenotypically similar to a range of TOR active site inhibitors, as well as an inhibitor of S6K1 (one of the direct targets of TOR) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The short root hair phenotype induced by AZD showed a synergistic interaction between AZD and 3OHPGSL.
source: Interestingly, the short root hair phenotype induced by AZD showed a synergistic interaction between AZD and 3OHPGSL suggesting that they may target different components of the TORC pathway that interact (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 7C.

claim: AZD induced a rounding of the root tip, but co-treatment with 3OHPGSL restored a wildtype-like tip phenotype.
source: AZD induced a rounding of the root tip (Dolan and Davies, 2004), but co-treatment with 3OHPGSL restored a wildtype-like tip phenotype (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 7D and citation to previous research.

claim: Active TOR negatively regulates autophagy across eukaryotic species including Arabidopsis.
source: For example, active TOR negatively regulates autophagy across eukaryotic species including Arabidopsis (Liu and Bassham, 2010; Shibutani and Yoshimori, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The atg5-1 mutant enhanced 3OHPGSL responsiveness.
source: We found that atg5-1 enhanced 3OHPGSL responsiveness (Figure 8A–B) while atg2-1 had a wild type response (Figure 8C–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A-B.

claim: The atg2-1 mutant had a wild type response to 3OHPGSL.
source: We found that atg5-1 enhanced 3OHPGSL responsiveness (Figure 8A–B) while atg2-1 had a wild type response (Figure 8C–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C-D.

claim: ATG5 has been shown to be involved in several forms of micro-autophagy whereas the role of ATG2 is more elusive and may not be required.
source: Micro-autophagy does not involve de novo assembly of autophagosomes, and ATG5 has been shown to be involved in several forms of micro-autophagy whereas the role of ATG2 is more elusive and may not be required (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Glucose is measured by two separate kinase systems that are oppositely repressed and activated to determine the potential growth capacity: SnRKs1 and TOR kinase.
source: Illustrating the key nature of metabolite measurement within plants is that glucose, is measured by two separate kinase systems that are oppositely repressed and activated to determine the potential growth capacity, SnRKs1 (sucrose non-fermenting 1 (SNF1)-related protein kinases 1) and the Target of Rapamycin (TOR) kinase (Sheen, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: SnRKs1s are evolutionarily conserved kinases that are activated when sugars are limiting.
source: SnRKs1s are evolutionarily conserved kinases that are activated when sugars are limiting (Lastdrager et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Arabidopsis thaliana has two catalytic SnRK1-subunits, KIN10 and KIN11.
source: Arabidopsis thaliana (Arabidopsis) has two catalytic SnRK1-subunits, KIN10 and KIN11 (SNF kinase homolog 10 and 11), that activate vast transcriptional responses to repress energy-consuming processes and promote catabolism (Baena-González, 2010; Crozet et al., 2014; Baena-González et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: KIN10 and KIN11 activate vast transcriptional responses to repress energy-consuming processes and promote catabolism.
source: Arabidopsis thaliana (Arabidopsis) has two catalytic SnRK1-subunits, KIN10 and KIN11 (SNF kinase homolog 10 and 11), that activate vast transcriptional responses to repress energy-consuming processes and promote catabolism (Baena-González, 2010; Crozet et al., 2014; Baena-González et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The TOR kinase is a central developmental regulator whose sugar-dependent activity controls a myriad of developmental processes including cell growth, cell-cycle, and cell-wall processes.
source: Oppositely, the TOR kinase is a central developmental regulator, whose sugar-dependent activity controls a myriad of developmental processes including cell growth, cell-cycle, and cell-wall processes.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about TOR function.

claim: The TOR pathway functions to modulate growth and metabolism by altering transcription, translation, primary and secondary metabolism, as well as autophagy.
source: The TOR pathway functions to modulate growth and metabolism by altering transcription, translation, primary and secondary metabolism, as well as autophagy (Sheen, 2014; Sablowski et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The TOR kinase primarily functions in meristematic regions where it promotes meristem proliferation.
source: The TOR kinase primarily functions in meristematic regions where it promotes meristem proliferation.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about TOR function.

claim: Within meristematic cell types, TOR measures the sugar content and if the tissue is low in sugar, TOR halts growth, even overruling hormone signals that would otherwise stimulate growth.
source: Within these cell types, TOR measures the sugar content and if the tissue is low in sugar, TOR halts growth, even overruling hormone signals that would otherwise stimulate growth (Xiong et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: In plants, TOR functions within a conserved complex that includes RAPTOR and LST8.
source: In plants, TOR functions within a conserved complex that includes RAPTOR (regulatory-associated protein of TOR) and LST8 (lethal with sec-13 protein 8) (Henriques et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: RAPTOR likely functions as an essential substrate-recruiting scaffold enabling TOR substrate phosphorylation.
source: RAPTOR likely functions as an essential substrate-recruiting scaffold enabling TOR substrate phosphorylation (Rexin et al., 2015), and LST8 is a seven WD40 repeats protein with unclear function (Moreau et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: LST8 is a seven WD40 repeats protein with unclear function.
source: RAPTOR likely functions as an essential substrate-recruiting scaffold enabling TOR substrate phosphorylation (Rexin et al., 2015), and LST8 is a seven WD40 repeats protein with unclear function (Moreau et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: TORC activity is positively linked with growth.
source: TOR complex (TORC) activity is positively linked with growth (Rexin et al., 2015) as mutants in any component lead to qualitative or quantitative defects in growth and development and even embryo arrest in strong loss-of-function alleles (Menand et al., 2002; Deprost et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mutants in any TORC component lead to qualitative or quantitative defects in growth and development and even embryo arrest in strong loss-of-function alleles.
source: TOR complex (TORC) activity is positively linked with growth (Rexin et al., 2015) as mutants in any component lead to qualitative or quantitative defects in growth and development and even embryo arrest in strong loss-of-function alleles (Menand et al., 2002; Deprost et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A key pathway controlled by TOR in all eukaryotes is autophagy.
source: A key pathway controlled by TOR in all eukaryotes is autophagy (Liu and Bassham, 2010; Shibutani and Yoshimori, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In non-stressed conditions, continuous autophagy allows the removal of unwanted cell components like damaged, aggregated or misfolded proteins by vacuolar/lysosomal degradation.
source: In non-stressed conditions, continuous autophagy allows the removal of unwanted cell components like damaged, aggregated or misfolded proteins by vacuolar/lysosomal degradation (Inoue et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Under low energy conditions, TORC inhibition leads to an induction of autophagy to free up energy and building blocks through degradation of cytosolic macromolecules and organelles.
source: Under low energy conditions, TORC inhibition leads to an induction of autophagy to free up energy and building blocks, through degradation of cytosolic macromolecules and organelles (Shibutani and Yoshimori, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Autophagy-mediated degradation is facilitated by formation of autophagosomes, which are double membrane structures that enclose cytoplasmic cargo and deliver it to the vacuole.
source: Autophagy-mediated degradation is facilitated by formation of autophagosomes; double membrane structures that enclose cytoplasmic cargo, and delivers it to the vacuole (Shibutani and Yoshimori, 2014; Feng et al., 2014; Le Bars et al., 2014; Zhuang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There are >120 known GSL structures limited to plants from the Brassicales order and some Euphorbiaceae family members.
source: There are >120 known GSL structures limited to plants from the Brassicales order and some Euphorbiaceae family members, with Arabidopsis containing at least 40 structures (Sønderby et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Arabidopsis contains at least 40 GSL structures.
source: There are >120 known GSL structures limited to plants from the Brassicales order and some Euphorbiaceae family members, with Arabidopsis containing at least 40 structures (Sønderby et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: GSLs, after conversion to an array of bioactive compounds, provide resistance against a broad suite of biotic attackers.
source: GSLs are amino acid derived defense metabolites that, after conversion to an array of bioactive compounds, provide resistance against a broad suite of biotic attackers (Sønderby et al., 2010; Lambrix et al., 2001; Kliebenstein et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mutants devoid of indole GSLs are unable to deposit PAMP-induced callose in cell walls via an unknown signal and pathway.
source: Tryptophan-derived indole GSLs or their breakdown products alter defense responses to non-host pathogens illustrated by biosynthetic mutants devoid of indole GSLs being unable to deposit PAMP-induced callose in cell walls via an unknown signal and pathway (Clay et al., 2009; Bednarek et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Indole GSL activation products have the ability to directly alter auxin perception by interacting with the TIR1 auxin receptor.
source: Similarly, indole GSL activation products have the ability to directly alter auxin perception by interacting with the TIR1 auxin receptor (Katz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Mutants in aliphatic GSL accumulation alter flowering time and circadian clock oscillations.
source: In contrast to indole GSLs, mutants in aliphatic GSL accumulation alter flowering time and circadian clock oscillations (Kerwin et al., 2011; Jensen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The aliphatic GSL activation product, allyl isothiocyanate can induce stomatal closure.
source: The aliphatic GSL activation product, allyl isothiocyanate can induce stomatal closure but it is unknown if this is specific to allylGSL or a broader GSL property (Khokon et al., 2011; Boller and Felix, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: AllylGSL can alter plant biomass and metabolism in Arabidopsis.
source: AllylGSL (other names are 2-propenylGSL and sinigrin) can also alter plant biomass and metabolism in Arabidopsis (Francisco et al., 2016a; Francisco et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Pseudomonad bacteria produce the evolutionarily young coronatine that alters the plant defense response by interacting with the conserved JA-Ile receptor COI1.
source: Pseudomonad bacteria produce the evolutionarily young coronatine that alters the plant defense response by interacting with the conserved JA-Ile receptor COI1 (Xie et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The plant polyphenol resveratrol directly inhibits the mammalian TOR to induce autophagy.
source: Similarly, an unknown phenolic metabolite appears to affect regulation of growth and development by influencing the Mediator complex that is conserved across all eukaryotes (Bonawitz et al., 2012; Bonawitz et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2014); and the plant polyphenol resveratrol directly inhibits the mammalian TOR to induce autophagy (Park et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The AOP3 enzyme that makes 3OHPGSL evolved prior to the split between A. thaliana and A. lyrata.
source: In the particular case of 3OHPGSL, the AOP3 enzyme that makes this compound evolved prior to the split between A. thaliana and A. lyrata suggesting that these species have had at least several million years/generations of potential to adapt.
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic relationships and enzyme evolution.

claim: Both allyl GSL and the GSL breakdown product indole-3-carbinol affect plant signaling and growth.
source: However; earlier studies have provided evidence that both allyl GSL and the GSL breakdown product indole-3-carbinol affect plant signaling and growth (Katz et al., 2015; Francisco et al., 2016a; Francisco et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In Arabidopsis there is one copy of TOR, and two copies of both RAPTOR and LST8 (RAPTOR1/RAPTOR2 and LST8-1/LST8-2).
source: In Arabidopsis- there is one copy of TOR, and two copies of both RAPTOR and LST8 (RAPTOR1/RAPTOR2 and LST8-1/LST8-2) (Moreau et al., 2012; Deprost et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: ATG2 is part of the ATG9 cycling system that is essential for autophagosome formation.
source: ATG2 is part of the ATG9 cycling system that is essential for autophagosome formation (Feng et al., 2014; Velikkakath et al., 2012; Ryabovol and Minibayeva, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: ATG5 is part of the dual ubiquitin-like conjugation systems responsible for ATG8 lipidation.
source: ATG5, is part of the dual ubiquitin-like conjugation systems responsible for ATG8 lipidation (Feng et al., 2014; Ryabovol and Minibayeva, 2016; Fujioka et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There are nine ATG8 paralogues in Arabidopsis.

claim: Micro-autophagy in animal systems has been shown to be negatively regulated by TOR.
